reason: A more carefully links each missing fact to the decision without treating product-market fit, business type, or investor goals as sufficient evidence on their own. It explicitly distinguishes an engineering-capacity shortage from poor prioritization and recommends neither investment when the bottleneck is unclear. B makes stronger unsupported leaps—for example, that product-market fit means distribution is now the constraint—and its default recommendation to spend 10–15% of cash on acquisition experiments is poorly justified when runway is short. A’s cost estimates are only rough assumptions, but its overall decision framework is better calibrated.
